nodes.label: Immanuel Wallerstein
nodes.date_label: Modern World-System I (1974), II (1980), III (1989), IV (2011) · World-Systems Analysis (2004)
nodes.description: A historian of the capitalist world-economy whose historical social science joins long-term change, a transnational division of labour and criticism of disciplinary boundaries. His definition of capitalism and treatment of class relations were disputed, including by Robert Brenner. His historical social science connects research and debate across sociology and history.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Modern World-System I–IV (1974, 1980, 1989, 2011); Historical Capitalism (1983); Unthinking Social Science (1991); Open the Social Sciences (collective Gulbenkian Commission report, 1996); World-Systems Analysis: An Introduction (2004). Volumes I–III revised with new prologues in 2011.
nodes.scope_note: The entry follows historical social science across disciplinary boundaries. Contributions are grounded in the scoped primary readings and attributed criticism; publication metadata supplies dates/credit only. Existing collective arrows, roster qualifications, field prose and source IDs remain. No complete Modern World-System volume, new prologue or other monograph has been read in this revision. Life dates are recorded separately; no work or influence interval is inferred.

edges.relationship: Makes the world-economy’s historical division of labour a unit for analyzing capitalist development.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1974 article, p. 399, read: agricultural production for market profit and a geographically differentiated division of labour are part of his definition. This is his contested account; it does not equate every dependency programme or claim free wage labour was universal.

edges.relationship: Intervenes in the transition controversy by disputing a definition of capitalism centered on the prevalence of wage labour.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1974 article, pp. 393 and 399, read: names Dobb/Sweezy and challenges Dobb’s definition. This is Wallerstein’s criticism, not a consensus description of Dobb; the old collective dependency→Dobb arrow remains.

edges.relationship: Treats historical social science as a challenge to fixed disciplinary boundaries and ahistorical universal laws.
edges.evidence_note: Williams’s framing (p. 203) and Wallerstein’s replies (pp. 206–207), read: historical systems, knowledge structures and disciplinary restructuring. The framing is attributed to Williams. A methodological contribution, without a founding claim or treating future-system predictions as established fact.

edges.relationship: Brenner charged Wallerstein’s world-system account with deriving capitalist development too directly from trade and the division of labour.
edges.evidence_note: Brenner’s 1977 critique, specifically §§II, IV and VI in the earlier accepted transcription reading, as documented in evidence-brenner.md §5. The publisher opening was newly read, but the full body was not independently reread here. This is Brenner’s charge; it does not replace Wallerstein’s own account or the existing collective critique of Frank, Sweezy and Wallerstein.

verification.note: Selected entries checked: MWS I (1974), II (1980), III (1989), their 2011 revised editions with new prologues; Historical Capitalism (1983), Unthinking Social Science (1991; second edition 2001), and Open the Social Sciences (1996, with the Gulbenkian Commission). Dates and credit only; no books read. MWS III is labeled by its unambiguous volume number because this list abbreviates its subtitle differently from the current publisher.

wallerstein_rise_primary.note: New limited rereading for Wallerstein biography: printed pp. 387–388, 393 and 399 OCRed from the existing linked scan and read. These pages address historical analysis, the Dobb/Sweezy issue, wage labour and agricultural capitalism. This does not expand the earlier reading to pp. 401–410 or constitute a full article/monograph reread; earlier qualifications are retained.

Collective critique edges are preserved.
